title: Ten weeks after launch
scenario:
You head customer success at a software company. 80 people in three teams got an AI assistant ten weeks ago. Access went out with one announcement email and a single enthusiastic champion, Dana.

The VP asks why use has dropped, and what to do about it. The exhibit shows the dashboard and a proposal.
exhibit:
AI assistant: week 10 (made-up example data)

Weekly active users (80 people have access)
  Week 2: 62   Week 4: 51   Week 6: 47   Week 8: 45   Week 10: 45

By team (week 10)
  Team       People with access     Active
  Team A     24                     22
  Team B     30                      9
  Team C     26                     14

Use cases (week 10)
  Use case            Active users    Messages
  Renewal prep        31              2,100
  Ticket summaries     3              1,900

Other facts
  Dana posted daily tips for 4 weeks, then went on leave. Posts stopped.
  VP proposal: "Each champion runs office hours for 5 hours a week."

questions.prompt: Which reading of the team table is best?

options.text: Team B has 9 of 30 active, so ask Team B's staff and manager what blocks use first.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's analytics page says dips can signal friction, and OpenAI's Insights page says to ask people with thin use how they work and where they struggle.

options.text: Team A at 22 of 24 is the target, so tell Teams B and C to copy Team A's messages.
options.explanation: Copying activity does not solve the problem. First find out why use is low in B and C.

options.text: Use is 45 of 80 overall, so the project is a success and the team table does not matter.
options.explanation: The overall number hides a gap. Active users fell from 62 to 45, and Team B is far behind.

options.text: Send all 35 inactive people a weekly reminder email, because reminders raise use.
options.explanation: 35 is right (80 minus 45), but reminders don't address what blocks people.

questions.prompt: Ticket summaries show 3 active users and 1,900 messages. What should you do?

options.text: Count it as the most successful use case, because 1,900 messages is a large number.
options.explanation: OpenAI's page says a message count doesn't tell you how much work the team finished.

options.text: Ask the 3 users what they do; they may have a workflow worth sharing.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's Insights page gives this exact advice for a category with few active users, and the Claude Code docs point to heavy users as people who can share techniques.

options.text: Cut the use case, because three users are too few to matter to the company.
options.explanation: Few users can mean a strong workflow that nobody else has seen. Ask before deciding.

options.text: Ask every other team to match the message volume of those three users from now on.
options.explanation: Copying volume copies activity, not method. Their technique is what the others need.

questions.prompt: Dana's posts stopped when she left. What does the champion kit say to do?

options.text: Ask Dana to keep posting from her leave, because the whole team depends on her.
options.explanation: That makes the single-person problem worse. The kit warns that adoption which depends on one person is fragile.

options.text: Wait until Dana returns, because only one person can be the champion of the team.
options.explanation: The kit says to name a second champion, so the habits don't depend on one person.

options.text: Name a second champion per team and set up weekly habits, like a thread and FAQ.
options.explanation: Right. The kit's four-week plan ends by naming a second champion and builds shared habits that continue without any one person.

options.text: Replace the tips with a longer monthly newsletter that is written by the VP.
options.explanation: The kit favors short, frequent examples where the team already reads, from peers.

questions.prompt: The VP wants each champion to run 5 hours of office hours a week. What is the best reply?

options.text: Agree, because more hours of support always lead to more use of the tool in the team.
options.explanation: The kit says the role should be a multiplier on existing work, not an additional support job.

options.text: Keep the core role near 40 minutes a week; add pairing only for blocked colleagues.
options.explanation: Right. The kit's budget is 15 + 20 + 5 = 40 minutes for the core work, plus optional pairing of 0 to 30 minutes.

options.text: Agree, but cut the weekly thread, because office hours replace the posting entirely.
options.explanation: The kit's thread costs about 5 minutes a week and keeps the team's content flowing.

options.text: Refuse; champions are volunteers, so they should help only when they have spare time.
options.explanation: The kit says the activities should fit in a normal working week, as a multiplier on existing work, not be left to spare time.
